paragraphs: Both wrappers were given the SQL, so the natural-language wording by itself does not explain this result. What matters is how each wrapper used the SQL. QuWARTS compiled it into a workload contract. In the archived DocETL path, the wrapper used SQL to choose the position and age columns and later ran that SQL in SQLite, but the extraction prompt itself received the separate natural-language question. The Frontcourt and Backcourt literals therefore reached the wrapper without becoming instructions to the mapper.

QuWARTS could see those two SQL literals when it built its workload contract, and the system produced both a raw table and a contract-mapped alternative. But the archived artifacts contain no position mapping rules, and the portfolio routed this question to the raw table anyway. That table contains forward, center, point guard, and similar labels, but not a single Frontcourt or Backcourt value. SQLite therefore removes all 160 rows before AVG is evaluated.

For this question, the DocETL runner creates one MapOp—the operator defined in §2.2.1—over the player documents. Its prompt asks for position and age and says to keep names “concise and normalized,” but it does not include the SQL literals, run Resolve (§2.2.3), or invoke the optimizer described in §4. The mapper returns ordinary detailed positions. The unchanged SQL then filters every one of them out.

A component swap would help only if it carries the missing semantics with it. Giving DocETL an explicit two-label taxonomy, or making QuWARTS produce and actually select its mapped view, should recover the two groups. It would not guarantee correct averages: QuWARTS is still missing age on 91 rows, and DocETL is missing many ages too. The clean test is to change positions only and leave every age untouched.

This question looks simple because it only groups and counts. In practice, nationality is an entity-resolution problem: Azerbaijan and American-born naturalized Azerbaijani may refer to the same benchmark category, while Nigerian and Nigerian-American may not. Exact SQL grouping cannot make that judgment.

This is the one question in the archived QuWARTS run that was routed to the contract-mapped table. Yet the mapped nationality column is identical to the raw one, and the archived artifacts contain no nationality mapping rules. That is important: selecting the mapped route did not mean that useful normalization had actually been learned. The result has 82 American players rather than 116 and splits several benchmark groups across alternate labels.

DocETL’s MapOp (§2.2.1 of the paper) extracts nationality independently for this question. The requested output type is only string. A serialized object such as {"nationality": "American"} is still text, so schema validation accepts it and SQL treats it as a new nationality. The paper describes Resolve specifically for canonicalizing keys in §2.2.3 and the optimizer that can synthesize such rewrites in §4. This benchmark runner uses neither; it is a single map followed by SQLite.

A working shared resolver would remove many extra and missing groups in both outputs. Moving QuWARTS’s mapping code exactly as it behaved here would not be enough, because it produced no useful change. Moving DocETL Resolve into the runner is more plausible, but it would still not recover empty nationalities or rows skipped after map errors. Canonicalization and coverage have to be measured separately.

The saved SQL is doing the requested join and average. The disagreement comes from the two tables it receives. Team is missing from 62 of QuWARTS’s 160 player rows, and NBA championship count is missing from 114. Even among the retained values, some team names or title counts do not match the benchmark. The exact join and AVG faithfully summarize that incomplete population.

QuWARTS’s shared database is economical because these player and team facts are extracted once for the whole workload. The downside is that a weak shared field remains weak for every question that uses it. Its miss=drop policy avoids inventing a number for an unknown championship count, but it also removes evidence and lowers coverage.

The DocETL runner rebuilds the player and team tables separately for this question. It explicitly instructs the model to use -1 for an unknown number, then coerces that value to a numeric column. That sentinel is a benchmark-runner choice, not a policy prescribed by the paper. The outcome is predictable: Celtics in one table does not equal Boston Celtics in the other, while -1 survives the join and lowers averages such as Brooklyn=-1.0. The paper defines Resolve in §2.2.3 and semantic Equijoin in §2.2.4, but this runner uses neither; it executes an ordinary SQLite equality join.

Two local changes would isolate most of DocETL’s avoidable error: turn -1 into NULL before SQL, and resolve the two team-name columns together. They would not repair incorrect championship facts. For QuWARTS, query-conditioned re-extraction of the missing team and title cells may improve recall, but replacing the shared extractor with DocETL’s per-question map would give up the reuse that produced the token advantage.

Here, normalization affects more than the name printed in the first column. The query keeps only colleges with more than one player. If UCLA and UCLA Bruins are separate strings, each group can fall below the HAVING threshold even though the combined college should qualify.

QuWARTS routes this question to its raw table. College is missing on 38 of 160 rows, MVP count is missing on 120, and no useful college resolver is applied before grouping. That explains both halves of the error: aliases alter which groups exist, while sparse MVP values alter the maximum inside the groups that survive.

DocETL again runs one query-specific MapOp (§2.2.1). It asks for concise names but supplies no common college vocabulary. Unknown MVP counts become -1—a choice in this runner, not in the paper—so a college with no recovered award value can still produce a numeric maximum of -1. The paper explicitly motivates inserting Resolve before Reduce for duplicate keys in §3.2.2. Here, however, aggregation is delegated directly to SQLite and the §4 optimizer is never asked to insert Resolve.

Running Resolve before the SQL GROUP BY should improve structure for both systems, and changing DocETL’s -1 values to NULL should remove the false maxima. Neither step fills in the many missing MVP counts. A fair ablation would first canonicalize college names on the archived rows, then repair MVP values in a separate run.

This SQL again requires the exact values Frontcourt and Backcourt. Both wrappers received that SQL, but neither turned the predicate into an enforced position mapping, so WHERE removes every row and SUM never sees an MVP value.

QuWARTS put the SQL literals in its contract but selected the raw configuration for this question. Its mapping machinery therefore did not protect the served table. In the archived DocETL path, SQL determined which columns to extract and was later used for SQLite closure, but the Map prompt received the separate natural-language question rather than the SQL text. “Normalize the name” was not an enforceable two-class mapping.

The paper’s Resolve operator (§2.2.3) is intended to merge alternate names of the same entity. Frontcourt and Backcourt are slightly different: they are a closed classification that maps several legitimate source categories into a coarser analytical vocabulary. Resolve could implement it if given the rule, but the generic operator cannot discover an unstated taxonomy reliably.

Adding the two-label mapping before SQL should restore the result shape in both systems. The totals may still be wrong because MVP count is missing on most player rows. That is why this should not be described as “moving the QuWARTS component fixes DocETL.” The taxonomy and the missing-value problem are independent.

QuWARTS reports six championships for the Canadian group because one retained player cell is supported by a passage about Larry Robinson’s six Stanley Cups. The value is grounded as a number, but it answers the wrong sports event. This is a semantic-role error, not a SQL MAX error.

The QuWARTS run recorded cell-verification decisions, but this question was served from the raw configuration. Quarantine also requires a confident contradicted or unsupported judgment; uncertainty is deliberately preserved. A type-valid count can therefore survive even when an audit record raises a concern. Hardening that gate would remove some bad cells, but without repair it would also create more missing values.

DocETL’s table has a different problem. The benchmark runner configures MapOp with skip_on_error=true, and only 116 of 141 player documents appear in the intermediate output. That setting belongs to this run; it is not a result claimed by the paper. Nationality aliases split more groups. Yet its American maximum of 9 is supported by Steve Kerr’s source row. The scorer marks it wrong because the saved gold result contains an empty string produced by mixed SQLite typing. That part is an evaluation artifact, not a DocETL extraction failure.

The paper describes user validations and retries in §2.1, gleaning in §3.2.1, and agent-generated plan validation in §4.2. This runner configures none of them; it only checks output shape and type. QuWARTS’s evidence verifier could provide a semantic check, but it must gate every serving route and trigger targeted repair. Even after either change, the American score should be reported separately until the gold-table typing issue is fixed.

The extra 2024 group in QuWARTS comes from Max Fiedler, who was undrafted. His document discusses the 2024 draft, and that nearby year was stored as his own draft year. The query then groups it correctly.

This is where QuWARTS’s evidence-oriented design should help, but the archived behavior shows the limit of a nonbinding check. A saved decision says the value is unsupported, while the raw served table still contains it. The verifier quarantines only confident negative judgments, and this question was routed to the raw configuration. Validation that is recorded but not enforced cannot protect the final query.

DocETL asks a single MapOp (§2.2.1 of the paper) to extract draft year from every player document. It does not run gleaning (§3.2.1) or configure the user validation and retry mechanism described in §2.1 to ask whether the year belongs to that player’s draft event. Unknown years become -1 under this runner’s prompt and are later removed by WHERE draft_year > 2010, so the sentinel is hidden in the final table. Plausible but unrelated years remain and move players into the wrong groups.

An evidence gate transplanted from QuWARTS to this DocETL map would help only if rejected values are retried with a more specific prompt. Conversely, DocETL gleaning could be added to QuWARTS’s extraction for disputed cells rather than rerunning every document. The first ablation should remove unsupported years; the second should re-extract only those cells and measure recovered coverage.

Both systems store a player’s team as one text field. The question asks for the current team, but the materialized row does not retain the date, roster status, or source event that made the team current. Once that context is gone, a later join cannot distinguish a present team from a historical one.

QuWARTS is missing team on 62 player rows and draft pick on 82. The shared relation graph knows that player.team joins team.team_name, but that structural edge does not make the extracted strings current or canonical. Exact SQL therefore groups incomplete and sometimes stale player records.

DocETL creates the player and team tables in two independent instances of the paper’s Map operator (§2.2.1). The player side contains full names such as Boston Celtics while the team side may contain Celtics. Some player rows also point to old teams. Resolve (§2.2.3) and Equijoin (§2.2.4) could reconcile fuzzy keys, but the benchmark runner bypasses them and uses SQLite equality.

Adding Resolve would recover some missed joins, but it could also confidently match a stale team to the corresponding franchise. The real fix needs two pieces: canonical franchise identity and an as-of rule backed by date or status evidence. Neither system currently has that complete component, so swapping only a resolver would be a partial repair.

Both outputs are empty because neither table contains the two position literals required by SQL. QuWARTS actually has medal values for 33 players, but none can reach AVG because the position predicate rejects every row.

Both wrappers received SQL containing Frontcourt and Backcourt. QuWARTS nevertheless selected its raw configuration. In the archived DocETL path, the wrapper used those SQL literals only in the later SQLite filter; the basic Map operator (§2.2.1) received the separate natural-language prompt with a generic normalization instruction, and the §4 optimizer was not invoked. Most DocETL positions and medal counts are also missing, but those weaknesses come after the all-row position failure.

This distinction matters when judging a component. A closed-vocabulary mapper would almost certainly improve structure by producing the two groups. It says nothing about whether the recovered averages would be accurate, because medal extraction remains sparse.

The smallest useful experiment is therefore not a full rerun. Apply a position mapping to the archived tables and leave every medal count unchanged. If the groups appear but the values remain poor, the taxonomy component fixed exactly what it was supposed to fix and no more.

This question counts NBA champions by college. A player can enter the wrong group because the college name is inconsistent, and can enter at all because a nonchampion was assigned a positive title count. The output shows both problems.

QuWARTS uses the raw table, where names such as Davidson and Davidson Wildcats remain separate and most championship cells are missing. Its type checks cannot tell whether a retained numeric count describes NBA titles rather than another achievement.

DocETL’s one MapOp (§2.2.1) extracts college and title count together, but the runner has no Resolve step (§2.2.3) and does not configure the user validations from §2.1. Unknown titles are -1 under the runner’s prompt and get removed by the at-least-one predicate; false positive titles remain. That is why several extra colleges are tied to players who are not NBA champions in the source table.

DocETL’s Resolve operator would address college aliases, while a QuWARTS-style evidence claim could address whether the title count has the right meaning. Neither component alone fixes the query. A two-by-two ablation—resolution on/off and event validation on/off—would show how much each contributes.

The striking totals—Indiana 1986, Los Angeles 2010, Miami 2025—are not arithmetic mistakes. Values such as 1986, 2010, and 2025 were extracted into the FIBA title-count column and then correctly passed the >=1 filter and SUM.

QuWARTS has a calendar-year-as-count check, but it is advisory and its name-based heuristic may not recognize fiba_world_cup as a count-like field. The cell verifier can also preserve lower-confidence negative judgments. Because this question is served from the raw configuration, a number that passes the scalar gate can reach SQL even when other audit evidence questions it.

The DocETL Map operator (§2.2.1) declares fiba_world_cup as a number. That guarantees parseable output, not semantic correctness. The runner supplies none of the user validations from §2.1, gleaning from §3.2.1, or optimized rewrites from §4. It also builds player and team names separately, so join-key mismatch removes some valid rows while bad counts inflate others.

A hard year-range gate would remove the catastrophic values in both systems, but it cannot recover the correct title counts. A complete repair would use a validator that asks whether the evidence states a FIBA World Cup win count, then retry rejected cells. Team-key resolution should be tested afterward as a separate source of error.

Tim Duncan’s 34 and Kobe Bryant’s 35 are real ages found in older articles. They are simply not the players’ ages in the benchmark’s 2026 reference frame. Those stale values wrongly let older players pass the 20-to-40 filter.

QuWARTS stores age as a scalar in its shared player table. It does not retain birth date or the date associated with the quoted age, so the serving layer cannot recompute or challenge the value later. Missing ages remove more players, and nationality aliases divide the remaining groups.

Neither the SQL nor the displayed question says “as of 2026.” The archived DocETL mapper therefore asks for age, not birth date plus a deterministic calculation. The paper’s rewrite directives (§3) and optimizer (§4) can decompose complex operations, while gleaning (§3.2.1) can critique an output; none can recover a reference date that is absent from the task given to the mapper.

This is not a useful component-swap case. Both systems need the same representation change: extract birth date with evidence, then calculate age at the declared reference date in code. A direct age extractor from either system preserves the ambiguity.

QuWARTS materializes 42 team rows from a 30-team corpus. Some rows are historical franchises; others are people or even a year treated as a team identity. Those extra identities create extra city groups and carry bad championship values into MAX.

DocETL’s runner asks for exactly one record from each team document. That simple cardinality prior is useful for this dataset: it avoids QuWARTS’s entity expansion and gives DocETL much better structure on this question. It still produces only 27 rows because map failures are skipped. The one-record rule and skip behavior come from this benchmark runner, not from a paper result.

The paper defines Reduce and Resolve in §2.2, Split and Gather in §2.3, and agentic optimization in §4. None was used here. The advantage comes from the hand-written runner’s one-document/one-row extraction shape, not from the paper’s optimizer.

Applying the same one-current-team-per-document constraint to QuWARTS would likely remove many spurious rows. It would not decide which fact in a historical document is current. That needs an as-of selection rule and evidence. Conversely, moving QuWARTS’s shared extraction into DocETL could improve reuse but would lose the helpful cardinality constraint unless it is made explicit.

DocETL marks unknown founding years as -1. The SQL predicate is founded_year < 1970, so -1 is not treated as missing—it is treated as a very early year. Charlotte, Miami, and New Orleans can therefore be counted even when the mapper did not recover a founding year.

This behavior comes directly from the runner’s prompt and numeric coercion, not from the paper’s design. The paper discusses validations and retries in §2.1 but does not prescribe -1 as a missing-number representation. Replacing -1 with NULL before SQLite would remove that specific error without changing extraction. Historical locations and wrong years would remain.

QuWARTS avoids the sentinel problem because its selected configuration drops missing values. Its shared team table instead contains too many identities and several wrong founding years, including 1976 for Houston and Philadelphia. Those values have the right type and therefore pass the raw scalar gate, but they fail the intended temporal meaning.

There is no single winning component to transplant. QuWARTS’s missing-value policy is clearly better for DocETL here. DocETL’s one-row-per-document shape could help QuWARTS’s extra-entity problem. Both still need a current-franchise resolver and a supported founding-year fact.

Before the gold query is executed, the case-study generator rewrites team ownership names using a separate owner table. The query shown to the systems asks only for the team table. Neither system is told to build or join the lookup that turns Dan Gilbert into Daniel Gilbert or Joseph Tsai into Joseph Chung-Hsin Tsai.

That makes part of the missing/extra group ledger an evaluation-contract problem. Document-grounded owner names can be reasonable and still fail exact comparison against the hidden rewrite. It is misleading to attribute all of this gap to normalization quality.

There are genuine system errors too. QuWARTS’s 42-row team table introduces historical and malformed owner identities, and some title totals are wrong. The benchmark’s DocETL runner skips four team documents and sometimes selects historical owners. Those errors should be discussed separately from the name-surface mismatch created by gold construction.

No component transfer can fix an undisclosed scoring rule fairly. The first comparison should score both outputs against owner names taken directly from the team source. A second, explicitly canonicalized evaluation can then test QuWARTS mapping or the paper’s Resolve operator (§2.2.3) on equal terms.

The query asks about teams in each city, which the benchmark interprets as current city and current championship total. Both extracted schemas store only location and championship. They omit the date or franchise period that would say which version of the fact is current.

QuWARTS reuses its oversized team table, so historical locations and extra identities become extra groups. DocETL’s one-row-per-document map avoids some expansion but can still choose St. Louis for Atlanta, New Jersey for Brooklyn, or Kansas City for Sacramento. Each answer is textually supported somewhere in the document.

A name resolver cannot safely solve this because the labels may refer to genuinely different periods, not alternate spellings of one simultaneous fact. The paper’s Resolve operator (§2.2.3) and QuWARTS’s contract mapping are therefore insufficient on their own.

Both pipelines need temporal candidates rather than a bare scalar: fact, franchise identity, start/end dates, and supporting passage. A deterministic current-as-of rule can then select one row. That is a schema and extraction redesign, not a component moved unchanged from one system to the other.

DocETL extracts 1959 as an owner’s age and uses -1 for five other unknown ages. SQLite averages all of them as ordinary numbers, producing an American average of 211.25. Output-schema validation is satisfied because every value is numeric.

The paper describes user validations and retries in §2.1 and agent-generated validation during optimization in §4.2. The benchmark runner configures neither. It runs only MapOp (§2.2.1) with skip_on_error=true and then hands the numeric column directly to SQLite. A NULL conversion and a plausible age range would remove the catastrophic arithmetic immediately.

QuWARTS does not have the sentinel failure, but its owner table contains only 11 rows and five ages are missing. Its American average is therefore based on too few people, while two nationality groups have no result. Dropping unknowns is safer than averaging -1, but it is not the same as recovering the data.

Moving QuWARTS’s missing-value policy into DocETL would clearly improve this output. It would not make either system complete. As with player age, the durable fix is to extract birth date and derive age at the benchmark date, with targeted retries for missing owners.

DocETL assigns Steve Ballmer’s 2000 Microsoft CEO year as a team-acquisition year. QuWARTS assigns Joseph Tsai 1996 even though its own saved evidence review does not support that as an ownership year. Both failures come from storing the year without the event that gives it meaning.

A numeric range cannot catch these values: 1996 and 2000 are perfectly plausible years. The validator has to ask a relational question—did this person acquire this team in this year?—and keep the supporting passage or event label.

DocETL’s map prompt does say what the question is about, but this runner performs one extraction attempt per document, with no gleaning (§3.2.1 of the paper) or user validation and retry rule (§2.1). QuWARTS has richer cell claims, yet the archived raw route still retained an unsupported value. One system lacks the check in this path; the other does not consistently enforce it.

A QuWARTS-style evidence claim would improve DocETL if it triggered retry rather than simply dropping the cell. DocETL gleaning could serve as that retry mechanism for QuWARTS too. Neither transfer recovers the many missing nationality and owner rows unless coverage repair is included.

QuWARTS produces all 22 state groups with no extras, so its structure is perfect on this question. Six averages are still wrong because the population scalar can come from a different year or from the larger metro area. Salt Lake City’s 1,257,936 instead of 200,133 is the clearest example.

The benchmark’s DocETL runner has a more basic coverage problem: nine state names are empty and eight populations are -1. The -1 convention comes from the runner’s prompt, not the paper. The final table hides those source rows because it only shows averages. In Florida, the valid Miami value is averaged with Orlando’s -1, yielding roughly half the expected population.

Converting -1 to NULL is a direct, high-confidence improvement for this runner. Adding the paper’s Resolve operator (§2.2.3) may recover some state-name variants, but it cannot fill an empty state or decide whether a population refers to a city or metro area. QuWARTS’s drop policy and broader state coverage are better here, while neither system represents population scope or date.

The next experiment should happen in two steps: first change only DocETL’s sentinel handling; then add explicit scope and as-of fields to both extractors. Combining those changes would hide which design choice produced the gain.

QuWARTS stores GDP as a bare number under a configuration whose unit strategy is none. Values expressed in dollars, millions, and billions therefore enter one column on incompatible scales. SQLite MAX simply chooses the largest representation.

DocETL’s output schema also asks for one numeric GDP field with no unit. Map (§2.2.1 of the paper) may return 518.5, 52,889, or 518,500,000,000 depending on how it interprets the source, and the runner’s type validation accepts every version. Blank state names remove more groups, while a metro population can wrongly admit a city through the one-million-person filter.

The paper’s optimizer (§4) can rewrite how a map is performed, but it cannot deterministically convert a unit that the output schema never retains. QuWARTS’s evidence and mapping machinery has the same limitation in this archived configuration.

This needs a richer record—GDP value, currency, scale, reference year, and supporting span—followed by code-based conversion. A resolver can still help DocETL’s state names, but that is a separate coverage fix. There is no existing component that can be copied across and recover units after they have already been erased.
